archetype.name: Rebuilding (offense ahead of defense)
archetype.definition: A second-year Kellen Moore team whose young quarterback has pulled the offense back toward league average while a defense that used to carry the franchise has collapsed, leaving a bottom-six roster by net efficiency.

report.headline: Shough's offense grew up; the defense fell apart, and the turnovers sank them
report.take:
These Saints are not the team of the last few years flipped upside down by bad luck. They are a different team, period. For most of the post-2020 decline the defense kept New Orleans respectable while the offense sputtered: last year the offense ranked 27th in EPA and the defense 10th. This year Tyler Shough has started every game, the offense has climbed to 21st in EPA and 23.1 points a game (17th), and the defense has dropped to 27th in EPA allowed. The record is 2-5, the point differential implies three wins, and net EPA ranks 27th. They are roughly as bad as they look, and only slightly unlucky.

The offense is a passing operation with no ground floor. Protection has held up (pressure rate allowed 11th, sack rate 13th), Chris Olave is the clear focal point with 71 targets, and Shough has shown the range: 410 passing yards at Detroit, positive double-digit pass EPA at Baltimore and against Pittsburgh. The run game is the anchor dragging it down: 3.13 yards a carry and a 32.5% success rate both rank 30th, and against Pittsburgh 18 rushing yards and -7.1 rush EPA wasted one of Shough's best passing days in a 10-16 loss. Kendre Miller, Alvin Kamara and, lately, Travis Etienne have all taken turns without fixing it, which points to the blocking more than the backs. Yards before contact rank 22nd.

The defense is the bigger problem, and it is broad. It ranks dead last in rush EPA allowed and 31st in success rate allowed, 29th on third down and 31st in EPA on deep passes. Atlanta ran for 205 yards and scored 45. The one thing it does well is finish: sack rate ranks 9th even though pressure rate ranks 27th. That gap usually narrows, so the pass rush is probably playing a bit over its head. The other swing has been turnovers. Thirteen giveaways have produced a -4 margin, and three of the losses came with three or four giveaways. Both wins came in games where they protected the ball, and the Giants win leaned on four takeaways and five sacks.

Where this goes depends on whether the turnovers settle down, because the efficiency underneath them is roughly league-average on offense and well below it on defense. The NFC South is weak enough to keep things interesting, with nobody above .500. But a defense this leaky against the run and on third down doesn't usually turn around in-season, and the schedule gets harder in the middle before easing late.

strengths.title: Clean pocket for a young passer
strengths.body: The line has kept Shough upright better than most: pressure and sack rates allowed both sit in the top half of the league. That has let the offense score more than last year's version despite a broken run game. The concern is depth, since right guard Cesar Ruiz, a 90% snap starter, is listed out.

strengths.title: Real offensive progress over 2025
strengths.body: Offensive EPA has moved from 27th last season to 21st, and the passing game has had several high-end days. Shough's ceiling games, at Detroit and against Pittsburgh, show the passing game can carry an offense. With Olave drawing a dominant target share and Jordyn Tyson nearing a return from IR, the passing side should stay roughly where it is.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: The Saints convert pressure into sacks at an unusual clip: sack rate ranks 9th while pressure rate ranks 27th. It is a genuine weapon against bad protection, but finishing at that rate on so little pressure tends to regress toward the pressure number.

concerns.title: Run defense is the league's worst
concerns.body: Opponents are gaining positive EPA per run, which almost no defense allows. Combined with a 31st-ranked success rate allowed and 29th on third down, offenses stay on schedule and keep drives alive. This is a structural flaw, not a fluke: it has shown up against good and middling offenses alike. Nathan Shepherd's illness thins the interior further.

concerns.title: Giveaways decided the losses
concerns.body: Thirteen turnovers have left a -4 margin, and the multi-turnover games at Detroit, against Las Vegas and against Minnesota were all losses. Some of this is a young quarterback pressing behind a run game that can't stay on schedule, so it may ease, but it is the single biggest driver of the record.

concerns.title: No functional run game
concerns.body: Bottom-three yards per carry and success rate make the offense one-dimensional, and on some days the run game actively loses games. Rotating three backs hasn't helped, which points at blocking and design. With Ruiz out, it is unlikely to get better soon.

trend.note: The results have swung on turnovers more than on any steady trend: a clean upset at Baltimore, a 45-point blowout by Atlanta, a turnover-fueled win at the Giants, then a low-scoring loss to Pittsburgh where good passing was undone by a dead run game.

nextGame.headline: A lucky 5-2 Browns team brings a real defense
nextGame.body:
Cleveland's record overstates its football. The Browns have the league's 2nd-largest wins over expected, have won most of their one-score games and have a negative point differential. Their offense ranks 24th in EPA behind a line that allows sacks at the league's worst rate. The defense is legitimate, though: 7th in EPA allowed, 6th against the pass, with 20 sacks. So this sets up as Shough's passing game against a good pass defense, and the Saints' finishing pass rush against a quarterback who gets dropped constantly. The Saints are at home in the dome, off a bye. Cleveland's offense can't run well either, so New Orleans' worst-in-the-league run defense may not get punished the way it did by Atlanta.

Availability leans on both lines. For New Orleans, guard Cesar Ruiz (knee) and DT Nathan Shepherd (illness) were listed out, and safety Justin Reid, a 93% snap starter, left the Pittsburgh game with a concussion. All three carry return estimates for this game, which are estimates, not promises. Rookie receiver Jordyn Tyson is on IR but described as getting closer. For Cleveland, guard Teven Jenkins is on IR into late November, and tackle Tytus Howard was being evaluated for a concussion. DT Mike Hall Jr. (ankle) and corner Myles Harden (hamstring) were also on the report. A thinner Browns line against this pass rush matters most.

waysToWin.title: Sack Watson behind a leaky line
waysToWin.body: The Browns allow sacks at the league's highest rate and are missing Jenkins, possibly Howard too. The Saints finish pressure efficiently. Drive-killing sacks are the cleanest way to hold a 24th-ranked offense in check and protect a defense that struggles on third down.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden-yardage game
waysToWin.body: Cleveland commits penalties at the 3rd-highest rate and its special teams have cost it EPA. If Shough doesn't give the ball away, a sloppy opponent with a weak offense is the kind the Saints can outscore, as they did in their clean win at Baltimore.

waysToWin.title: Hit the explosive run lanes
waysToWin.body: Cleveland's defense allows explosive runs at the league's highest rate and misses tackles often. The Saints' run game is poor on a down-to-down basis, but a couple of breakaway carries from Miller or Kamara could open up an offense otherwise facing a top-six pass defense.

waysToLose.title: Shough forced into mistakes
waysToLose.body: Against a pass defense this good, with a run game that can't take pressure off, Shough may need to force throws. The Minnesota game, 96 passing yards and three turnovers against the league's top defense, is the template for this going wrong.

waysToLose.title: Third downs extend Browns drives
waysToLose.body: Even a weak offense can grind out points when the defense allows conversions at a bottom-four rate and allows positive EPA per run. If Cleveland stays ahead of the chains and avoids sacks, its offense doesn't need to be good, and the Browns win another close game.

waysToLose.title: Deep shots against the secondary
waysToLose.body: The Saints are 31st in EPA on deep passes, and Reid's status in the back end is uncertain. One or two completions downfield can swing a game the Browns would otherwise struggle to win on sustained drives.

nextGame.watch: The Saints' sack count against a Browns line allowing sacks at the league's worst rate, and whether chasing those sacks leaves the deep middle open.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency profile points to a team that loses more than it wins. The good news is that the record is only modestly worse than the point differential, so there is no big bounce owed by luck, and the remaining schedule is mixed: a stretch at Chicago and Cincinnati and home against Green Bay, then two games with a Tampa Bay offense ranked 28th and a home date with 2-5 Arizona. A weak NFC South keeps the division in view longer than a 2-5 team deserves.

The passing offense looks sustainable, and Tyson's return could lift it. The pass rush's sack finishing likely cools. The run defense and third-down defense have shown no sign of fixing themselves. If the turnover rate regresses toward normal, the Saints win some of the coin-flip games they've been losing. If it doesn't, this is a five-win team again.
swingFactors: Run defense against Carolina and Atlanta
Jordyn Tyson's return and Ruiz's health on the line

confidence.note: Seven games with a stable QB, but turnovers and injuries on both lines add noise.
